1.1.note: Numerator from national accounts; denominator (agricultural employment) is an ILO modeled estimate, and the 2025 observation is a current-year estimate rather than a final national-accounts outturn. Next level not proposed: Level 5 requires exceeding 10,000. Egypt's 2025 figure of 8,942.42 is below that cut by roughly 1,058 units, and no retrieved source publishes an Egypt value above 10,000 on this or any other basis — the highest historical Egypt figure in the supplied pages is 7,680 (constant 2010 US$, 2019, IndexMundi/T5). Egypt sits below the Arab World aggregate for the same series (10,945.1 in 2025), which itself only crosses the 10,000 cut. Additionally, no current-USD figure is published, and had one been available it would more likely push the value down than up given exchange-rate depreciation, so there is no basis for reaching level 5. The indicator name says "Agriculture value added per worker (USD)" with no sector scope or price basis. The only published figure for Egypt is WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD, whose definition is broader and more specific than the name: it covers "Agriculture, forestry, and fishing" (ISIC Rev.4 divisions 01-03) and is denominated in constant 2015 US$, not current USD. So the recorded 8,942.42 is (a) agriculture+forestry+fishing, not agriculture alone, and (b) a constant-price, not a current-price, dollar figure. A current-US$ per-worker figure for Egypt is not published in the retrieved pages, and the divergence matters for Egypt given the large post-2016 and post-2022 exchange-rate depreciation — a current-USD denomination would very likely place Egypt materially lower. Related but non-substitutable figures on the same pages: Egypt agriculture, forestry and fishing value added (constant 2015 US$) = 52,746.55 million in 2025; employment in agriculture = 18% of total employment in 2025. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI NV.AGR.EMPL.KD): 8942.42 for 2025.

1.3.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Employment in agriculture (% of total employment) (modeled ILO estimate), Egypt, Arab Rep.
1.3.note: ILO modeled estimate / nowcast for 2025, not a nationally reported observation; WDI metadata warns that imputed observations 'are subject to high uncertainty, and should not be used for country comparisons or rankings'. The country page rounds to whole percent (18); the T5 aggregator TradingEconomics reports 18.69% for 2023 from the same World Bank collection. Next level not proposed: Level 4 requires employment in agriculture below the 15% cut. Egypt's most recent published value is 18% (2025 ILO modeled estimate), above 15; no source in the supplied pages publishes any Egyptian figure below 15% for this construct — the nearest alternative datapoint, 18.69% for 2023, is higher still. The evidence therefore does not show Egypt's agricultural employment share having crossed the 15% threshold. The indicator name 'Employment in agriculture (%)' omits its denominator; the quoted series is explicitly '% of total employment', which is the standard reading and is what is recorded here. Two residual definitional gaps, both flagged in the assessment's own census note: (i) the sector is ISIC-A, i.e. 'activities in agriculture, hunting, forestry and fishing' (WDI metadata), so it is broader than agriculture alone — forestry and fishing employment is included in the 18%; (ii) the 2025 datapoint is an ILO MODELLED nowcast rather than an Egyptian labor force survey observation, so it should not be treated as a 'Measured' national statistic. No CAPMAS labor force survey figure for Egypt was present in the supplied pages to cross-check; the ILOSTAT Egypt country profile page returned a Cloudflare bot-verification screen with no data. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SL.AGR.EMPL.ZS (ILO modeled estimate)) reports 17.52 for 2025, which differs from the value recorded here.

1.6.value: DATA GAP — Worked through the ten supplied pages in order. Sources 1, 2, 3 and 4 (IFAD, T1): the 2017 CSPE, the 2025 CSPE presentation, the 2025-2030 COSOP and the IOE workshop note — searched for any percentage attached to markets, marketing, value chains or contract farming; found only the COSOP's 18.5 per cent workforce / 95 per cent landholdings figures and qualitative CSPE ratings ('weak market linkages and financial inclusion', 'critical gaps remained in marketing and rural finance'), none of which is an access rate. Source 5 (PRISMA) mentions an evaluation synthesis titled 'Smallholder Access to Markets' but only in a table of contents, with no Egypt figure. Source 6 (FAO family farming page) was blocked by a bot-verification screen and yielded no text. Source 8 (FAO/CIHEAM/CIRAD small-scale family farming, Egypt, T2) retrieved text stops at the table of contents; the marketing sections that might carry a figure are not in the supplied text. Source 7 (IFPRI/AgEcon, T2) is the paper matching the census note about contract-farming participation, but the supplied excerpt (title page, abstract, introduction) states no participation percentage and describes a sub-national irrigated-agriculture sample. Source 9 (GIZ, T4) is a qualitative industrial scan of six Upper Egypt governorates with no prevalence rate in the supplied text. Source 10 (LinkedIn, T5) is promotional and admissible for existence only. Conclusion: no quote-verifiable figure for the named construct exists in the supplied pages; cell held rather than filled.
1.6.note: Next level not proposed: Level withheld rather than set at 1: the evidence does not show that smallholder access to formal markets is below 20 per cent, nor above it. The qualitative IFAD CSPE finding of weak market linkages and the IFPRI framing that participation 'remains low in Africa' are directional, not calibrated to any threshold, and neither is a measurement of the Egyptian national smallholder population. The indicator names national SMALLHOLDER ACCESS to FORMAL MARKETS as a percentage. The best available Egyptian evidence in the retrieved pages is (a) an IFPRI working paper on smallholder participation in profitable value chains and contract farming based on an irrigated-agriculture survey, i.e. a PARTICIPATION rate in a specific marketing arrangement rather than ACCESS to formal markets, and not national in coverage; (b) a GIZ industrial scan of willingness to source from smallholders in six Upper Egypt governorates (Minya, Beni Suef and others), again sub-national and qualitative; (c) IFAD's 2025-2030 COSOP, which reports that smallholder farmers 'constitute 18.5 per cent of the national workforce and operate 95 per cent of agricultural landholdings' — structural shares of workforce and landholdings, not market access; and (d) the 2025 CSPE finding of 'weak market linkages and financial inclusion', a qualitative rating. Each of these sits on the wrong side of the unratified definitional question flagged in the indicator census: participation/willingness-to-source in selected governorates is not national access, and no publisher in these pages converts it into an access percentage.
1.6.defnote: The name asserts national smallholder ACCESS to formal markets; Egypt records a regional contract-farming PARTICIPATION rate from seven governorates and Nigeria a 2012/13 channel-of-sale share — two different constructs, neither of which is access, and neither national in Egypt's case.
1.6.name: Smallholder access to formal markets (%)

1.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO Statistics highlight 'Credit to agriculture. Global and regional trends 2014-2023' — checked for a country-level penetration measure; it reports only global/regional credit volumes and agriculture's share of total credit, naming China and India, not Egypt. 2) CAPMAS press release on agricultural sector cooperative activity 2018/2019 — the most on-point national source; gives loan values by maturity and cooperative counts, but no share of farmers served. 3) CAPMAS 'Agricultural Property and Rein 2017' catalog entry — metadata landing page only, documentation not rendered, no credit variable listed. 4) FAO microdata catalog, Egypt Agricultural Census 2009-2010 — scope list covers holdings characteristics, cultivated area, irrigation, employment, machinery, livestock; credit is not among the enumerated topics, so the census as documented does not yield a credit-access rate. 5) World Bank Microdata Library, Global Findex 2025 Egypt — variable dictionary only (1001 cases, 199 variables); relevant variables exist (borrowed, fin22a, fin23, urbanicity, receive_agriculture) but no estimates are printed on the page, and the underlying unit is adults 15+, not farmers. 6) FAO/CIHEAM 'Small-scale family farming in the Near East and North Africa: Egypt' — only front matter and table of contents were returned; no credit-access figure appeared in the retrieved text. 7) CIHEAM 1995 chapter on credit and investment in Egyptian agriculture — abstract-level content, gives a 50 percent cost-coverage statistic for PBDAC loans, which is a different construct and long out of date. Dead ends: no FAOSTAT Egypt credit-to-agriculture country row, no Findex tabulated rural/farmer borrowing value, no agricultural census credit module in the supplied pages.
1.7.note: Next level not proposed: Withholding rather than scoring: no source in the retrieved set reports any numerator (farmers or holdings with agricultural credit) over any denominator (total farmers or holdings) for Egypt. Even the lowest rung would require a figure demonstrably below 10 percent for farmers, and none exists here; the CAPMAS loan totals and the Findex variable list cannot be arithmetically reduced to such a share. Named construct = share of FARMERS with ACCESS to agricultural credit. Nearest available evidence for Egypt in the supplied pages: (a) CAPMAS annual bulletin on agricultural cooperative activity — total investment loans granted to farmers of 13.8 billion pounds in 2018/2019 versus 14.2 billion in 2017/2018, with 4310 agricultural credit cooperative associations; this is a monetary flow and an institution count, with no denominator of farmers, so it cannot be converted to a percentage. (b) Global Findex 2025 Egypt microdata holds 'borrowed', 'fin22a Borrowed from a formal bank or similar financial institution' and an 'urbanicity' rural flag, i.e. borrowing behavior of rural adults 15+ (a population including non-farmers), which is on the wrong side of the census's open definitional question in two ways at once: wrong unit (adults, not farmers) and wrong concept (use, not access). No value was published on the retrieved page in any event. (c) The 1995 CIHEAM chapter states PBDAC loans 'cover only 50% of production costs' — a coverage-of-costs ratio for borrowers, not a share of farmers borrowing, and three decades stale.
1.7.defnote: The name asserts a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS; Egypt records rural adults aged 15+ (a population that includes non-farmers) and Nigeria records smallholder households, and both measure borrowing/use rather than access.
1.7.name: Agricultural credit access (% farmers)

1.8.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all nine supplied pages in order. (1) World Bank PAD5035 Emergency Food Security and Resilience Support Project — CSA appears only in the acronym list and thematic framing in the retrieved extract; no adoption percentage in the text provided. (2) FAO SCALA Egypt country page — policy/NDC/NAP narrative, vulnerability and emissions shares (15 percent of Delta arable land affected, 31.2 percent of population in agriculture) but no CSA adoption figure. (3) FAO Country Investment Highlights No. 22, 'Climate-smart policies to enhance Egypt's agrifood system performance and sustainability' — retrieved text is front matter and contents only; chapter 4 on scaling up CSA technologies is listed but its numbers are not in the extract. (4) FAO 'Transformation to low carbon agrifood value chains in Egypt' (SAIL) landing page — abstract cites 173 Farmer Field Schools, no adoption rate. (5) FAO/EBRD Egypt Wheat Sector Review 2015 — front matter and contents only, no CSA adoption. (6) FAO Climate-smart agriculture case studies 2021 — Egypt appears as a SAIL financing case study on page 57; the retrieved text is contents only, no percentage. (7) ICARDA/CGIAR technical report on mechanized raised-bed adoption in Sharkia and Assiut — the nearest quantified Egyptian CSA adoption material, but it is wheat AREA under one practice in two governorates and the table values themselves are absent from the retrieved text. (8) USDA FAS Grain and Feed Annual EG2025-0009 — confirms government promotion of raised-bed cultivation and its water/seed savings, but no share of farmers or area adopting. (9) Al-Ahram Weekly feature (T5) — qualitative farmer testimony and FAO report summary; T5 cannot carry a statistic in any case. Dead ends: no CAPMAS or MALR statistical output was among the supplied pages, and no FAOSTAT/WDI series measures climate-smart practice adoption. Concluded found=false with a ratification hold.
1.8.note: Next level not proposed: Level 1 was not proposed because the evidence does not establish that adoption is below 20 percent any more than it establishes any other band — there is simply no measured share of Egyptian farmers using climate-smart practices in the retrieved sources. What would be required: a national survey (e.g. CAPMAS/MALR agricultural survey, or an FAO/World Bank household survey) reporting the proportion of agricultural holders applying one or more defined climate-smart practices. The indicator names the percentage of FARMERS adopting climate-smart practices (a basket of practices, national scope). The only quantified Egyptian material in the retrieved evidence is area-based and practice-specific: the ICARDA report (T2, Dhehibi et al. 2017) tabulates the relative importance of wheat AREA under mechanized raised-bed (MRB) farming in Sharkia governorate 2013-2017, based on a purposive sample of 80 farmers per governorate (40 adopters / 40 non-adopters by design, so the sample split is not an adoption rate). USDA FAS (T3) confirms raised-bed cultivation is being promoted nationally and 'reduces water consumption by 25 percent, requires 15 percent less seeds' but gives no adoption share. FAO's SAIL-derived study reports work across '173 Farmer Field Schools' — an activity count, not a coverage percentage. All three differ from the named construct on unit of measurement (land/schools vs farmers), practice basket (one practice vs climate-smart practices generally) and geography (two governorates / project sites vs national).
1.8.defnote: The name counts FARMERS adopting climate-smart practices; Egypt records a share of WHEAT AREA under a single practice and Nigeria a share of farmers in two zones adopting at least one climate-resilient crop TRAIT — land, practice-basket and geographic scope all differ from the name.
1.8.name: Farmers using climate-smart practices (%)

8.1.src: World Bank, World Development Indicators — Prevalence of undernourishment (% of population), Egypt, Arab Rep. (source: FAO)
8.1.note: FAO model-based estimate; the World Bank portal displays the series rounded to whole percent (a secondary aggregator, TheGlobalEconomy.com, reports the unrounded FAO figure as 9.4 for 2023). FAO's 2023 values are projections based on nowcasts. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require the published prevalence to fall below 7.5 percent. It does not: the World Bank/FAO figure for Egypt in 2023 is 9 percent (9.4 percent unrounded per the FAO-sourced aggregator), i.e. above the 7.5 cut, and the trend is upward (8.8 percent in 2022 per the aggregator). The older WHO NLiS profile figure of 4.5 percent for 2016-2018 would clear the 7.5 cut, but it is an outdated vintage of the same FAO series and FAO explicitly instructs that only the current series be used, including for past years; it therefore cannot support level 4. The World Bank indicator SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS is FAO's Prevalence of Undernourishment (PoU), the share of the population whose habitual dietary energy consumption is insufficient — exactly the named construct, at national level for Egypt. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS) reports 9.4 for 2023, which differs from the value recorded here.
8.1.tier_detail: FAO model-based estimate; the World Bank portal displays the series rounded to whole percent (a secondary aggregator, TheGlobalEconomy.com, reports the unrounded FAO figure as 9.4 for 2023). FAO's 2023 values are projections based on nowcasts.
8.1.name: Prevalence of undernourishment (%)

8.5.note: RATIFICATION HOLD — The retrieved evidence counts female agricultural HOLDERS (the person making the major management decisions on the holding), not female LANDOWNERS. This is exactly the open definitional question flagged for this row: the indicator name says women who OWN land, while the available canonical statistic counts operators, who may rent rather than own. Egypt's own census shows the two are not identical: of 3 717 991 holdings with land, 3 256 384 were 'Owned' and 223 118 'Rented from others' (1999/2000), but that tenure breakdown is NOT sex-disaggregated in the published main results. The indicator's own unit, '(% holders)', points back at the holder-based statistic, which is why this is recorded rather than abstained; the reader should treat it as a holder share, not an ownership share. No published Egyptian percentage figure (as opposed to counts) for either construct was found in the supplied pages.. The level is withheld and this row leaves every mean. Dated census (1999/2000 round); the counts are published as absolute numbers, not as a percentage, so any share is a derivation rather than a published statistic. 2.1.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU Statistics landing page — confirms ITU publishes population covered by mobile-broadband network 'total and by urban/rural area', but only as global/regional/development-group aggregates, not per-country. 2) ITU DataHub home and About pages — confirm the World Telecommunication Indicators questionnaire collects 'mobile population coverage (total, 3G, 4G and above)'; no rural disaggregation requested from countries; no Egypt value on these pages. 3) ITU DataHub UMC dashboard page — rendered for United States, not Egypt; no rural coverage indicator in the UMC target set anyway. 4) ITU Digital Development Dashboard for Egypt (ddd_EGY.pdf) — the only Egypt-specific coverage data found: national 100% (>=3G) and 98% (>=4G) for 2022; the only rural cut on the page is households with internet access at home (64%), a different construct. 5) MCIT Egypt indicators index and the September 2023 ICT Indicators in Brief (T3) — mobile penetration, subscriptions, ADSL regional distribution and number of rural local exchanges (1072 fixed-line exchanges in rural areas), but no rural mobile broadband population coverage percentage. 6) GSMA Coverage Maps page and GSMA State of Mobile Internet Connectivity 2025 (both T4) — methodology and global/regional coverage-gap discussion only; no Egypt rural figure quotable, and T4 is inadmissible for this prerequisite row. 7) nPerf Egypt coverage map (T5) — crowdsourced map, no statistic, inadmissible. Dead end: no admissible source in the retrieved set states rural 3G/4G coverage for Egypt.
2.1.note: Context figure is a national (not rural) administrative estimate reported by the national regulator/ministry to ITU; coverage-by-technology data are operator-reported footprints, not measured service availability. Next level not proposed: Even the highest defensible rung cannot be argued: the evidence does not show any measurement of coverage restricted to rural population in Egypt. To score level 5 (>80) one would need a published rural coverage percentage above 80; the ITU country dashboard supplies only an undifferentiated national figure, and the ITU urban/rural coverage series exists solely as world/regional/income-group aggregates, not as an Egypt observation. The indicator names RURAL mobile broadband coverage. The best available Egypt-specific evidence in the retrieved pages is NATIONAL: ITU's Digital Development Dashboard for Egypt reports population covered by at least a 3G mobile network (2022) = 100% and at least a 4G mobile network (2022) = 98%. These are total-population figures with no urban/rural split. The only rural-disaggregated Egyptian figure on the same ITU page is a different construct entirely — households with Internet access at home, rural (2022) 64% (vs urban 84%) — which measures household subscription/access, not network coverage. ITU states it publishes coverage 'by urban/rural area' only as global and regional aggregates ('Population covered by a mobile-cellular and a mobile-broadband network, total and by urban/rural area'), not as an Egypt country value in any page supplied here. This is precisely the open question flagged in the indicator census: Egypt's row currently sits on the wrong side of it, carrying the ITU national at-least-3G number as if it were a rural measure.
2.1.defnote: The name asserts RURAL coverage, but Egypt's row records the ITU national at-least-3G figure as a clean cls="Measured" number that scores level 5 mechanically, while Nigeria records a rural-but-4G-only modelled estimate — so the register's only universal connectivity prerequisite carries a…
2.1.name: Rural mobile broadband coverage (3G/4G)

2.5.src: ITU DataHub — ICT prices dashboard, Egypt (Affordability, %GNI pc)
2.5.note: Basket price collected from operator tariffs by ITU/national regulator; allowance definition changed in the 2025 methodology revision (5GB headline basket), so the series is not strictly comparable with pre-2025 2GB-era figures. Next level not proposed: Level 5 was not proposed because the published value does not fall below the final cut of 1 per cent: ITU records 1.58% for the data-only 5GB basket, and the only Egypt basket that does fall below 1% (the 1GB low-consumption voice-and-data basket at 0.74%) is a smaller-allowance, voice-inclusive basket and therefore not the mobile broadband data basket this row names. No source in the retrieved pages shows Egypt's mobile broadband basket under 1% of GNI pc. The indicator name 'Mobile broadband price (% GNI pc)' does not fix the allowance, the basket type, or whether the denominator is monthly or annual GNI pc. The figure recorded is ITU's live 2025 headline series: the data-only mobile-broadband basket of 5GB, expressed as a percentage of MONTHLY GNI per capita (ITU's standard affordability convention). Two adjacent ITU baskets exist for Egypt in the same 2025 dashboard and would give different numbers under a different reading of the name: the mobile data-and-voice low-consumption basket (70 min, 50 SMS, 1 GB) at 0.74% and the mobile data-and-voice high-consumption basket (140 min, 20 SMS, 5 GB) at 1.92%. No 2GB data-only basket is published for 2025 (ITU retired it in the 2024 methodology revision), so if the row is ratified as a 2GB basket the figure here is on the wrong side of that question and would need to be re-sourced from the legacy 2021-2024 series. For a data-only mobile broadband basket read monthly, 1.58% is the correct and current ITU figure for Egypt.

2.7.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU DataHub Egypt page for household indicators with Location disaggregation — only 'Households with Internet access at home' rural (64.1%, 2022); no smartphone ownership indicator. 2) ITU Digital Development Dashboard PDF for Egypt (ddd_EGY.pdf) — checked the 'Mobile phone ownership' block: only 'Individuals owning a mobile phone (2022) 97%' plus female/male splits, all national and all 'mobile phone' rather than smartphone; the rural disaggregation on that page applies only to household internet access. 3) ITU WTID list of tables — confirmed table 49 'Individuals using a smart phone by gender and urban-rural location' exists as a series and that Egypt's in-scope population is 15-74, but the page is a table list only and carries no Egypt values, and the series measures use not ownership. 4) ITU Statistics landing page and Yearbook 2018 page — navigational only, no country values. 5) ITU model-questionnaire presentation — confirms the household ICT indicator set includes HH18 'Own a mobile pone' but no smartphone-ownership-by-location indicator; methodological, no data. 6) MCIT Indicators listing page (T3) — lists ICT Indicators in Brief, Quarterly Bulletin and the household ICT survey products but exposes no rural smartphone figure in the page text. 7) MCIT ICT Indicators in Brief September 2023 PDF — mobile subscriptions, penetration, ADSL regional distribution and rural local exchanges only; no smartphone ownership. 8) Ahram Online summary of the March 2026 ICT Bulletin (T5) — rural/urban split given only for fixed-line subscriptions; no smartphone ownership, and T5 cannot carry a statistic in any case. Dead end: no CAPMAS or MCIT household ICT survey tabulation with an urban/rural smartphone ownership breakdown was among the supplied pages.
2.7.note: Next level not proposed: The evidence does not show any figure whose denominator is the rural population (or rural households) of Egypt and whose numerator is smartphone ownership. 5.4.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the two IFPRI/CGIAR items that name digital literacy among Egyptian smallholder farmers (Policy Note 23, Sept 2024; IFPRI Discussion Paper 02359, Sept 2025; and the CGSpace record for the Food Policy 2026 article) — these carry the RCT baseline barrier percentages (54/52/49/19/16/14) and treatment effects (uptake +20 pp, utilization +18–26 pp, trust +8–13 pp), but no digital-literacy prevalence rate. 2) Checked the Wageningen (edepot) preprint of the same Food Policy article — same abstract, no prevalence figure in supplied text. 3) Checked the World Bank Egypt Digital Economy Country Assessment (T1) — supplied text is copyright page and table of contents only; a 'Digital Skills' section is listed but its content, and any farmer-specific figure, is not in the retrieved text. 4) Checked the World Bank agri-solar baseline diagnostic (2018) — supplied text is front matter/abstract on off-grid solar entrepreneurship, no digital-literacy data. 5) Checked ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' (CGSpace record) — abstract mentions 'knowledge levels of farmers' as a constraint qualitatively; item is Limited Access and no figure is available. 6) Checked the OUCI index record for Mansour (2023), ICT use among 131 farmers in Qena — abstract notes illiteracy and lack of knowledge affect ICT use, but the record contains no digital-literacy percentage and the study is 131 respondents in one governorate. 7) ScienceDirect page returned a captcha, no text. Dead ends: no CAPMAS, ITU or Findex farmer-disaggregated digital-skills figure appeared among the supplied pages.
5.4.note: Non-representative purposive sample: ~4,000 farmers in two Upper Egypt governorates who are members of GIZ-supported farmer organizations; intervention sample further restricted to the 2,400 smartphone owners. Baseline item is self-reported perception of barriers, not a tested literacy measure. Next level not proposed: Even level 1 (a value below 10) cannot be asserted, because no figure for the named construct exists at all; and no level above 1 can be argued because there is no representative measurement — the 52 percent barrier figure is a two-governorate, self-reported, inverse-direction item, not a national literacy rate. What is missing for any level is a nationally scoped measurement of farmers' digital skills (e.g., a CAPMAS or MALR survey module, or an ITU-style digital-skills indicator disaggregated to agricultural households). The indicator names a national percentage of farmers who ARE digitally literate. The available evidence (IFPRI/GIZ RCT baseline, Minya and Benisuef, 2024) reports that 52 percent of sampled farmers cited 'general digital literacy' / 'farmer digital illiteracy' as a key challenge to using mobile applications, alongside 54 percent citing unawareness of applications and 49 percent citing lack of smartphone access. This is (a) the inverse direction (illiteracy as a barrier, not literacy attainment), (b) self-reported perception rather than assessed skill, and (c) sub-national and non-representative (two governorates, farmer-organization members). Related context also in the pages but not the construct: of 3,332 full-time farmers in the sample, 2,400 own smartphones and 950 do not; and the RCT reports training effects (uptake +20 pp, utilization +18–26 pp, trust +8–13 pp), which are adoption outcomes, not a literacy stock. The World Bank Egypt Digital Economy Country Assessment page retrieved contains only front matter and a contents listing for a 'Digital Skills' chapter, with no farmer digital-literacy figure in the supplied text.
5.4.defnote: The name asserts a national digital-literacy rate among farmers, but Nigeria records rural-population digital skills and Egypt records a two-governorate RCT baseline whose headline figure is digital ILliteracy, the inverse of the indicator's H direction.
5.4.name: Digital literacy among farmers (%)

8.9.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all ten supplied pages in order of likely relevance to a national smallholder reach figure. (1) FAO Digital Services Portfolio country cases — Egypt section describes El Mufeed's participatory design and promotional campaign but publishes no user counts or coverage share (numbers given are for Senegal, a different country, and therefore inadmissible here). (2) and (3) World Bank Egypt Digital Economy Country Assessment (two PDF renderings) — the retrieved text is front matter and table of contents only; no agriculture or smallholder reach figure appears in the supplied text. (4) ICARDA 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' — abstract only, Limited Access record; states sensors and mobile apps are 'fairly widely used' and names Al Mufeed, Hudhud, DAIRS, but gives no percentage and no smallholder denominator. (5) IFPRI policy note on app developers — qualitative interview study; states many Egyptian tools remain pilot-stage or region-specific with very few at national scale; no reach figure. (6), (7), (8) IFPRI policy note and Discussion Paper 02359 on the digital literacy RCT — the only numbers found: 4,000 target farmers in Minya and Beni Suef, 3,332 full-time, 2,400 smartphone owners; baseline barrier percentages; treatment effects of +20 pp uptake, +26/+18 pp utilization, +8-13 pp trust. All sample-bound, none national. (9) GSMA AgriTech Accelerator report — cohort and impact framework; implementation countries listed do not include Egypt in the retrieved text, and no Egypt figure appears. (10) Food Policy article (WUR repository copy) — same RCT; adds that in Egypt 'uptake of these technologies remains low' qualitatively and cites a continent-level figure on smallholder internet access from Mehrabi et al., which is Africa-wide, not Egypt. Dead ends: no national statistical office (CAPMAS) agricultural digital-use release, no Ministry of Agriculture registry/e-extension user count, and no FAO/World Bank indicator with a smallholder denominator was among the supplied pages. Conclusion: figure not present in the supplied evidence; abstaining rather than substituting the sub-national RCT figures.
8.9.note: Next level not proposed: Even level 1 is not supported: no source in the retrieved set states any percentage of Egyptian smallholders reached by, registered on, or actively using digital agricultural services at national scope. The qualitative finding that uptake 'remains low' and that tools are mostly pilot-stage is consistent with a sub-10-percent national share but does not establish one, and the indicator's cut points cannot be applied to a qualitative statement without inventing a denominator. Closest evidence, as context only, none of it a national smallholder reach share: (1) IFPRI Policy Note / Discussion Paper 02359 and the Food Policy article (Abdelaziz & Abay), https://cgspace.cgiar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/81b8d4be-61c7-470a-9b12-52a0c51d2d4c/content and https://cgspace.cgiar.org/server/api/core/bitstreams/a95d7429-19f8-4a76-8152-06c499fce4a0/content — target population is about 4,000 smallholder farmers in Minya and Beni Suef belonging to around 30 GIZ-supported farmer organizations; of 4,000, 3,332 are full-time farmers and 2,400 own smartphones, so the intervention sample was restricted to smartphone owners. Baseline barrier shares (54% unaware of existing apps, 52% digital illiteracy, 49% lack of smartphone access) describe that project sample, not Egypt's smallholder population. Treatment effects (uptake +20 percentage points; utilization +26 pp in the discussion paper, +18 pp in the journal version; trust +8-13 pp) are experimental impacts, not reach levels. (2) IFPRI policy note on app developers and ICARDA's 'Current Situation of Digital Agriculture in Egypt' both state qualitatively that Egyptian digital agriculture tools remain largely pilot-stage or region-specific with very few achieving national scale, and that uptake remains low — directional, but no percentage. (3) FAO's Digital Services Portfolio page describes the El Mufeed app rollout in Egypt from 2019 with no user or coverage figures. On the indicator's own open question: the name asserts a national share of smallholders 'reached', and none of the retrieved evidence sits on that side of the question — the available numbers are sample-level and 'reached' is undefined (registered vs. active vs. benefiting) in every source.
8.9.defnote: The name asserts a national share of smallholders reached, but Egypt's scored level 1 is derived from a two-governorate RCT baseline explicitly labelled as having no national provenance, and "reached" is nowhere defined against registered, active, or benefiting users.

The nearest adjacent evidence — the IFAD Egypt CSPE (2017-2023 portfolio, US$646.3 million, five projects) — does document income and productivity outcomes for rural households, but the attributed causes are irrigation rehabilitation, rural finance, farmer field schools and market linkages, not digital agriculture tools. The World Bank 2021 report 'Accelerating the transformation of Egypt's agri-food system' lists a section 5.5 'Digital Technologies', but the retrieved text is front matter and table of contents only and carries no yield or income figure for digital technology adoption. Judged against the indicator's name, which fixes the outcome as yield or income, none of the retrieved evidence measures the named construct for digital agriculture; the census's own caveat (that Egypt's level 3 rests on an evaluation measuring diffusion and adoption rather than yield or income) is confirmed rather than resolved by these pages.

8.17.value: DATA GAP — Reviewed all nine supplied pages in order. Sources 1 and 3 (FAO geodata toolkit; FAO WEPS-NENA Egypt results) returned FAO 404 error pages with no content. Source 2 (FAO e-Agriculture, 2019) describes the launch of a digital agricultural extension model and CALR agrometeorological data but gives no user or reach numbers. Source 4 (World Bank PID P180480, 2024) states the objective of strengthening nation-wide agriculture information systems and early warning services and gives macro/poverty statistics (32.5% national poverty, 66% of poor rural, 42% working poor in agriculture) but no advisory reach figure. Source 5 (WFP Egypt brochure landing page) gives Upper Egypt livelihood shares (63% of employment, 40% of rural income, 85%/60% of rural households) — livelihood dependence, not advisory reach; the PDF itself was not supplied. Source 6 (MDPI Sustainability, Kassem et al. 2019) is the only farmer-survey percentage available (51.9% with no climate change knowledge, two Nile Delta governorates, n=792) — wrong construct and sub-national. Source 7 (USU DigitalCommons mirror of the same paper) was CAPTCHA-blocked. Sources 8 and 9 (WMO/EMA) are purely supply-side: NAP climate scenarios, early-warning system support, EW4All flood forecasting training — no coverage statistic. Dead end: no ITU/FAO/national statistical office figure on farmer advisory receipt for Egypt appeared in the retrieved set.
8.17.src: CGIAR/IFPRI, Climate-smart agriculture and development practices in Egypt: Report on a policy seminar event
8.17.note: Provenance adjusted on second review: The first pass was too strong in recording a complete gap. Source 7 affirmatively states that the Bashaer platform delivers tailored climate-smart recommendations directly to farmers in Egypt. It does not, however, support a numerical climate-advisory reach percentage or a scored threshold level. Next level not proposed: Withholding rather than proposing a level: no source in the retrieved set reports the share, count, or coverage rate of Egyptian farmers receiving climate/weather advisories. The 51.9 percent unaware figure is an awareness measure from two governorates and cannot be inverted into 48.1 percent advisory reach — awareness of climate change is not receipt of an advisory service, and the sample is not national. The closest quantified evidence is Kassem et al. (2019, Sustainability 11(3):685), a survey of 792 farmers in two Nile Delta governorates reporting that 51.9% of surveyed farmers had no knowledge about the climate change phenomenon. That is (a) climate-change awareness, not receipt of a climate advisory service, (b) a two-governorate sample rather than a national figure, and (c) dated 2019. It cannot be read as 'climate advisory reach'. On the census's open question, all Egypt-specific material retrieved sits on the SUPPLY side: the World Bank Climate Resilient Agri-Food Transformation Project (P180480, US$250m, 2024) has as a development objective 'to strengthen the nation-wide agriculture information system and early warning services'; EMA/WMO material describes supporting climate change early warning systems and agricultural forecasting under the NAP; FAO describes a digital agricultural extension model piloted on citrus, date palm, poultry and nutrition. None of these state how many or what share of farmers receive advisories.
8.17.tier_detail: Policy-seminar report summarizing participant statements; it provides no recipient enumeration, denominator, or survey method.
8.17.defnote: Does the indicator measure farmer receipt of advisories, or supply-side issuance (warnings issued, platforms live), which is all either country publishes?

A1-CAND-IMP.value: DATA GAP — 1) FAO GIEWS Egypt country brief (T1) — read in full; gives 2026/27 cereal import requirements of 29 million tonnes, wheat 13.5 Mt, maize 15.5 Mt, plus 2026 wheat production ~10 Mt, but publishes no dependency ratio; a ratio derived from these would be my own arithmetic, not a published figure, so rejected. 2) UNdata mirror of FAOSTAT item 21035, 'Cereal import dependency ratio (percent) (3-year average)' (T1) — exact construct match; Egypt is listed in the 226-country filter and 19 year-windows are offered, but the rendered table shows only records 1 of 4004 through Albania 2007-2009, so the Egypt rows were not in the fetched text. Dead end for quoting. 3) FAO data catalog entry for the Suite of Food Security Indicators (T1) — metadata only, no country values. 4) FAOSTAT landing page (T1) — update log only, confirms Suite of Food Security Indicators refreshed 21 July 2026; no values. 5) FAO Statistics Country Profile Tool (T1) — describes a dashboard that would carry the Egypt value, but the page itself contains no data. 6) FAO openknowledge figure_52 PDF, 'Cereal import dependency ratio, top countries (2020-2022)' (T2) — right indicator and vintage, but the country list is the top 20 (Antigua and Barbuda, Barbados, Djibouti, Dominica, Grenada, Libya, Malta, Republic of Moldova, Solomon Islands, Bahamas, Jamaica, Micronesia, Jordan, Cyprus, United Arab Emirates, Saint Lucia, Kuwait, Trinidad and Tobago, Vanuatu, Cabo Verde); Egypt is absent. Note Libya and Jordan appear here — neighbouring-country figures, explicitly not carried across the border to Egypt. 7) CGIAR-hosted FAO RNE presentation 'Food security in Egypt' (T2) — names 'Cereal import dependency ratio (percent) (3-year average)' as an Egypt stability indicator and shows a chart with a 0-70 axis, but the underlying values are in the figure, not the extracted text; unquotable. 8) Heliyon article via PMC — concerns wheat import dependency and econometric elasticities, a different construct from the FAO cereal import dependency ratio. 9) Food Systems Dashboard table — blocked by a Vercel security checkpoint, no data returned; also T5. Conclusion: correct series located at T1, Egypt value not retrievable from supplied pages; abstaining rather than estimating.
A1-CAND-IMP.note: Correct series identified (FAOSTAT Suite of Food Security Indicators, item 21035) but the Egypt data row was not returned in the retrieved page text; re-query with the Egypt country filter applied. Next level not proposed: No level proposed because the indicator is a carried candidate (non-scored) and, independently, no quote-verifiable Egypt figure exists in the supplied pages. The named construct is the cereal import dependency ratio in percent — (cereal imports − cereal exports) / (production + imports − exports) — a 3-year-average FAOSTAT stability indicator. The only Egypt-specific cereal-trade quantities in the supplied pages are FAO GIEWS import REQUIREMENTS in physical volume: 'Cereal import requirements for the 2026/27 marketing year (July/June) are forecast at 29 million tonnes', with wheat at 13.5 million tonnes and maize at 15.5 million tonnes. Those are tonnage forecasts, not a percentage dependency ratio, and cannot be converted into one without the domestic supply denominator, which is not on any supplied page. Offered as context only, not as the value.

A1-CAND-IRR.note: Dated reference year (2002); AQUASTAT figure derived from Ministry of Agriculture and Land Reclamation agricultural statistics. Egypt's area equipped for irrigation and cultivated area are reported as identical (3 422 178 ha), so the ratio is 100% by construction. Next level not proposed: Not applicable: scoring is withheld by design for carried candidate indicators. The residual evidentiary gap is temporal, not conceptual — no post-2002 AQUASTAT value for 'area equipped for irrigation as % of cultivated area' appears in the supplied pages. The AQUASTAT line 'Total area equipped for irrigation ... as % of cultivated area' is exactly the named construct (area equipped for irrigation divided by cultivated area). Note that a more recent AQUASTAT 2016 country profile (Source 7) reports cultivated area of 3 761 000 ha for 2013, but the retrieved excerpt of that document does not include the corresponding area-equipped-for-irrigation table, so the 2002 figure is the most recent quotable value in the supplied pages. A T5 aggregator page (ReportLinker) states 99.63% for 2023, but that is expressed as a percent of AGRICULTURAL land, not cultivated area, and is a non-admissible tier for a statistic.
